analysis.one_liner: Lifts all campaign contribution limits, ends public financing of presidential campaigns, and expands disclosure.
analysis.headline: Introduced with six Republican cosponsors including Speaker Hastert and Majority Leader DeLay, the bill never received a committee or floor vote and died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would remove every limit on how much anyone can give to a federal candidate or party starting in 2005, on the theory that unlimited money plus instant disclosure is freer speech. It would also shut down the presidential public financing system funded by the voluntary $3 tax checkoff, ending the matching-fund program after 2004 and sweeping any leftover money into the Treasury. In exchange, it would require faster and fuller disclosure: electronic filing for everyone, 24-hour reporting of every contribution in the final 90 days before an election, and state and local party reports filed with the FEC.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy donors and large contributors would gain the ability to give unlimited amounts directly to candidates and parties. Political parties would gain unrestricted fundraising power. Anyone following money in politics would gain from stricter, faster disclosure, and small donors who use the presidential checkoff would lose their voluntary $3 option.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes all federal contribution limits for contributions made after 2004, allowing donors of any means to give unlimited amounts directly to candidates and parties.
It requires all campaign reports to be filed electronically and posted on the internet, making contribution data available to the public much faster.

It requires campaigns to report every contribution received in the final 90 days before an election within 24 hours, and strips away the 'best efforts' exception for identifying contributors giving more than $200 a year, so big donors cannot stay hidden behind late or sloppy reporting.
It would require state and local party committees to file copies of their state-law disbursement reports with the FEC, widening the public record of party money.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary voters would bear the cost of a system where the loudest financial voices belong to the biggest checks, since unlimited contributions concentrate influence in the hands of the wealthiest donors. Taxpayers would lose the option to direct $3 to presidential campaigns, and candidates who relied on public matching funds would lose that support.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary voters and small-dollar checkoff taxpayers

drawbacks.text: With all contribution limits removed, a single donor could give more money directly to one candidate in one election than tens of thousands of ordinary donors combined, magnifying the political voice of the wealthiest Americans relative to everyone else.

Terminating the Presidential Election Campaign Fund and the matching payment program after 2004 eliminates the one voluntary, public channel that lets presidential candidates run without relying on large private donors, and sweeps any remaining checkoff money into the general Treasury.

Requiring every contribution of any size to be reported within 24 hours during the final 90 days of a campaign would impose a heavy administrative burden on volunteer-run and small-dollar campaigns, the very challengers the bill says it wants to help.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The disclosure provisions are genuine improvements: electronic filing, 24-hour reporting, and filing state party reports with the FEC would make campaign money visible faster. But those gains are paired with the bill's centerpiece — eliminating every contribution limit — which would hand the largest direct financial influence to the wealthiest donors, and with ending presidential public financing, which removes a low-cost alternative to privately funded campaigns. On balance, the trade favors large donors over small ones, and the transparency upgrades do not offset that shift.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, neither ever acted on it, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. John Doolittle introduced the bill on November 19, 2003, joined at introduction by six Republican cosponsors including Speaker Dennis Hastert and Majority Leader Tom DeLay.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on House Administration and the Committee on Ways and Means.
Neither committee took any further action on the bill before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, so it never received a markup or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal contribution limits and the presidential public financing system stayed in place, and large donors did not gain the ability to give unlimited amounts directly to candidates. The disclosure improvements it contained were lost as well.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing contribution limits and public financing survived.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, including the two top House leaders; no Democrat supported it, and the Republican-controlled committees never moved it.

industries.industry: Wealthy donors and large political contributors
industries.note: After 2004, the bill would let any donor give unlimited amounts directly to federal candidates and parties. Its gain — outsized influence through the biggest checks — comes directly at the cost of ordinary voters' equal voice in elections.

Parties could raise unlimited contributions, though they would also face new disclosure duties, including filing state and local reports with the FEC and 24-hour reporting of late contributions. The fundraising upside and the concentration of money in party and big-donor hands would come at the cost of a level financial playing field.

industries.industry: Publicly financed presidential campaigns and small-dollar checkoff taxpayers
industries.note: The bill terminates the $3 tax checkoff after 2003 and the Presidential Election Campaign Fund and matching payment account after 2004. This eliminates the one channel that let candidates run for president without depending on large private donors.

industries.industry: Campaign filing software and compliance services
industries.note: Mandatory electronic filing for every campaign committee would create steady demand for filing software and compliance help. The same mandate makes contribution data public faster, so the industry's gain runs alongside a public benefit.
